title: Separate the event from the verdict
summary: Help your teen distinguish a specific difficulty from a conclusion about their whole character or future.

details.content: When an assignment remains unfinished, your teen may experience it as evidence that they are lazy or incapable. Keeping the event specific leaves room to understand what happened while acknowledging how painful it feels. Your own explanation also needs room for your teen to correct it.

Your teen says, "I didn't finish the essay; I'm useless." Instead of replying, "You're a great student; that's ridiculous," try, "That sounds really painful. The essay is unfinished, and it sounds as though that now says something about your whole self; have I understood?"

content: Acknowledge the pain before examining the conclusion.
Describe the observable event without adding a character label.
Check your own assumptions about effort, caring, or motivation.
Name the possible shift tentatively and welcome correction.
Keep your care available whether or not the task gets finished.

title: Notice and check the shift
summary: Listen for a difficulty becoming broader or more permanent, and gently check what your teen means.

details.content: A change from "this assignment" to "everything" or from "today" to "always" may signal that a difficulty is expanding into a broader judgment. Your teen's familiar expressions and the surrounding context matter more than a fixed list of phrases. Noticing a possible shift gives you something to check together.

Your teen says, "I wasted today; I'll never manage college." Instead of responding, "You're catastrophizing again," try, "It sounds as though today has become a prediction about college; is that what you mean, or am I missing something?"

content: Listen for shifts from a specific event to a judgment about everything.
Notice when a present difficulty becomes a permanent prediction.
Use your teen's own words when checking your understanding.
Accept a correction without arguing for your interpretation.
Agree on early signals during a calm conversation rather than monitoring every mood.

title: Receive before redirecting
summary: Acknowledge your teen's experience and give them room before offering explanations, reassurance, or solutions.

details.content: An explanation or solution offered before your teen feels heard may come across as dismissal. You can recognize disappointment, shame, or exhaustion while leaving a harsh self-judgment open. Giving your teen room also helps you learn what this particular moment is like for them.

Your teen says, "I tried all afternoon and got nowhere." Instead of responding, "Just break it into smaller steps," try, "You've spent hours trying, and you're still stuck; that sounds exhausting," then pause before offering help.

content: Reflect the experience briefly in words that sound natural to you.
Use tentative language when naming a feeling.
Ask one question at a time and leave room for an answer.
Offer listening or quiet company without requiring an explanation.
Repair a dismissive response by acknowledging it and asking less.

title: Notice what your responses communicate
summary: Examine the expectations and urgency your teen may hear through comparisons, repeated attention, tone, and body language.

details.content: Your teen may hear standards in your comments about other children, the achievements you dwell on, or the roles you assign within your family. Your pace, expression, and physical presence may also communicate pressure when you intend to reassure. Their interpretation is something to ask about, and a repair becomes more credible when your everyday responses change too.

You have repeatedly praised another family's college admissions and your teen has become quiet. Instead of adding, "I just want you to reach your potential," try, "I've brought up other people's admissions a lot; I wonder how that's been landing with you," then make time to listen without defending your intention.

content: Notice the expectations behind your praise, comparisons, and family labels.
Ask how comments about other children land with your teen.
Show interest in your teen's experiences beyond achievement.
Check your voice, expression, pace, and distance for unintended pressure.
Acknowledge a mismatch and change a recurring response your teen finds pressuring.

title: Pause the verdict and offer choice
summary: Invite your teen to leave harsh self-judgments undecided while choosing a usable form of support.

details.content: A conversation about self-worth can become an argument when your teen feels compelled to defend how bad things are. A temporary pause in the verdict leaves room without requiring immediate optimism. Offering a small choice helps your teen retain a say in what happens next.

Your teen says, "This proves I'll never succeed." Instead of insisting, "Tell me three reasons that isn't true," try, "Could we leave what this means about your future open for now?" Pause, then offer, "Would you prefer listening, quiet company, or help with the situation?"

content: Invite a temporary pause in conclusions about identity or the future.
Avoid requiring your teen to agree with a positive description of themselves.
Offer two or three realistic support choices.
Let your teen decline a phrase or an option without having to defend the choice.
Ask permission before returning to the original task.

title: Match support to available capacity
summary: Adjust the amount of talking and problem-solving to what your teen can use in the moment.

details.content: Your teen may be able to collaborate at one point and feel overwhelmed by questions a little later. As intensity rises, fewer words, lower stimulation, and familiar support may be more usable. Established treatment and safety arrangements take priority when the situation reaches their agreed thresholds.

Your teen says, "I can't think; stop asking me things." Instead of continuing to explain how to start the assignment, try, "I'll stop the questions; I'm here," then allow a pause and use the support preferences you agreed on together.

content: Check whether your teen wants practical help before offering it.
Shorten your sentences and reduce questions as overwhelm increases.
Pause the task and analysis when your teen cannot use them.
Use familiar support and respect preferences about proximity, eye contact, and touch.
Stop discussing the task and follow the established safety arrangement when its threshold is reached.

title: Build a shared support map
summary: Agree during calmer moments on early signs, preferred support, unhelpful responses, and when to involve others.

details.content: A shared map gives you and your teen a way to prepare before a difficult moment. It protects your teen's say in the support offered and makes space for other trusted people and existing treatment arrangements. The agreement can change when a phrase or approach stops being useful.

During a calm conversation, instead of announcing, "Next time I'll tell you when you're spiraling," try, "Would it be useful to agree on a way I can check in when things get painful?" If your teen agrees, choose the wording and support options together.

content: Choose a calm time and ask whether your teen wants to make a support map.
Agree on a brief cue your teen finds acceptable, or leave it out.
List preferred support options and responses your teen wants you to avoid.
Clarify other support roles and treatment or safety thresholds with the treating team as appropriate.
Revisit the map and keep room for privacy and changing preferences.

title: Review gently and adjust together
summary: After recovery, learn from the sequence together and choose one workable adjustment without creating another trial of character.

details.content: Your teen may feel depleted or exposed after a difficult episode, even when the intensity has fallen. A later, agreed review can help you identify what added pressure, what helped, and what to change. Earlier signals, preserved connection, and easier repair are meaningful forms of progress.

After a difficult homework evening, instead of asking immediately, "Why did you let it get that bad again?" try later, "Would now be a useful time to look briefly at what happened?" If your teen agrees, ask what helped and acknowledge any pressure you added.

content: Wait until your teen has recovered enough and agrees to a brief review.
Describe the sequence and your own contribution without assigning fault.
Notice what helped, including small changes in connection or intensity.
Choose one adjustment and ask what observations your teen wants shared with their clinician.
Arrange a separate conversation about remaining responsibilities and keep other supports involved.
